title: Dramatis Personae
focus: the cast and world of the play

teacherSummary.text: The cast list sets up two kingdoms (Scotland and England), King Duncan and his sons Malcolm and Donalbain, the generals Macbeth and Banquo, the thanes (Macduff, Lennox, Ross and others), Lady Macbeth and Lady Macduff, Hecate and three Witches, and apparitions. The play moves between Scottish castles, a heath, a battlefield and the English court.

context.history: Shakespeare wrote Macbeth around 1606, soon after James VI of Scotland became James I of England (1603). James claimed descent from Banquo, had written a book on witchcraft (Daemonologie, 1597) and had survived the Gunpowder Plot (1605). Shakespeare drew the story loosely from Holinshed's Chronicles (1587).

significance: A cast list is a map of power: who rules, who serves, who is family and who stands outside the human order (the Witches). Reading it first lets students track loyalty and betrayal from the first scene.
discussionQuestions: If someone told you that you would one day be king or queen, what would you do with that knowledge?
Where does setting appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with ambition and its costs?

items.prompt: Analyze how the cast list balances the political and the supernatural.
items.expected: Most entries are political: a king, his heirs, two generals, noblemen, an earl and officers, all defined by title and service. literaryElements.label: Characterization
literaryElements.explanation: The cast list already divides the world: a king and his sons, generals, thanes, the English allies, and at the bottom the women and the supernatural. Macbeth and Banquo share one title, "general of the king's army": they begin as equals, which makes their divergence the play's first test.

literaryElements.label: Setting
literaryElements.explanation: "Scotland; England": a divided map. England will be where the rightful heir and the forces of order gather.

themesAndDevelopment.development: almost all named roles are men defined by military or noble rank; the three women with lines are Lady Macbeth, Lady Macduff and the Gentlewoman, plus Hecate and the Witches, whose power is outside the social order.

evidence.quote: Macbeth, general of the king’s army
evidence.use: Macbeth's role is defined by service to the king, the bond he will break.

evidence.quote: Banquo, general of the king’s army
evidence.use: The identical title makes Banquo Macbeth's double and foil.
Listed among the "supernatural" roles; Shakespeare's text calls them "the weird sisters" (from the Old English wyrd, fate).

claimEvidenceReasoning.claim: The cast list sets Macbeth and Banquo up as equals so that the play can show two different responses to the same temptation.
claimEvidenceReasoning.evidence: Macbeth, general of the king’s army
claimEvidenceReasoning.reasoning: Both are listed as "general of the king's army," so when the witches speak to both, the difference in what they do will come from character, not position.

weDoAnswers: Same title, same rank; so any difference between them will be a choice. Expected link: fate and free will.
facilitation: Ask students to sort the cast into groups (royal family, thanes, outsiders, supernatural) and predict which groups will clash.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.

items.text: How does the characterization in “Dramatis Personae” shape what we understand about the cast and world of the play?

items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The cast list sets Macbeth and Banquo up as equals so that the play can show two different responses to the same temptation. Useful evidence: “Macbeth, general of the king’s army” (Dramatis Personae, line 4): Macbeth's role is defined by service to the king, the bond he will break. On characterization: The cast list already divides the world: a king and his sons, generals, thanes, the English allies, and at the bottom the women and the supernatural. Macbeth and Banquo share one title, "general of the king's army": they begin as equals, which makes their divergence the play's first test. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.
